title: Ἵππος καὶ βοῦς καὶ κύων καὶ ἄνθρωπος
titleEn: The Horse, the Ox, the Dog, and the Man
part: The Horse, the Ox, the Dog, and the Man (Chambry 139)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 139. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ζεὺς ἄνθρωπον ποιήσας ὀλιγοχρόνιον αὐτὸν ἐποίησεν.
sentences.tr: Zeus anthrōpon poiēsas oligochronion auton epoiēsen.
sentences.l: Zeus, having made man, made him short-lived.
sentences.n: ποιήσας … ἐποίησεν sets the same verb twice: the making and the terms of the making are one act. ὀλιγοχρόνιον is a predicate accusative with ἐποίησεν — "made him short-of-time", not "made a short-lived man".

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ συνέσει χρώμενος, ὅτε ἐνίστατο ὁ χειμών, οἶκον ἑαυτῷ κατεσκεύαζε καὶ ἐνταῦθα διέτριβε.
sentences.tr: Ho de tēi heautou synesei chrōmenos, hote enistato ho cheimōn, oikon heautōi kateskeuaze kai entautha dietribe.
sentences.l: But he, using his own understanding, when the winter set in, built himself a house and spent his time there.
sentences.i: But he, making use of the understanding that was his, would build himself a house whenever winter set in, and pass the time in it.
sentences.n: χράομαι takes the dative of the thing used (τῇ συνέσει). The imperfects ἐνίστατο, κατεσκεύαζε, διέτριβε are customary — not one winter but every winter, which is why the idiomatic line reads "whenever". σύνεσις is the power of putting things together, practical intelligence: man's one compensation for the short life just given him.

sentences.t: Καὶ δή ποτε σφοδροῦ κρύους γενομένου, καὶ τοῦ Διὸς ὕοντος, ἵππος ἀντέχειν μὴ δυνάμενος ἧκε δρομαῖος πρὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, καὶ τούτου ἐδεήθη ὅπως σκέπῃ αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē pote sphodrou kryous genomenou, kai tou Dios hyontos, hippos antechein mē dynamenos hēke dromaios pros ton anthrōpon, kai toutou edeēthē hopōs skepēi auton.
sentences.l: And indeed once, a violent frost having come on, and Zeus raining, a horse, not being able to hold out, came at a run to the man, and begged of him that he should shelter him.
sentences.i: And so one day, when a bitter frost had come on and Zeus was sending rain, a horse could not hold out; he came running to the man and begged him for shelter.
sentences.n: Two genitive absolutes stacked one on the other — the standard way this collection sets a scene. τοῦ Διὸς ὕοντος: Greek says "Zeus rains" where English says "it rains"; the god and the weather are not separable. δέομαι takes the genitive of the person entreated (τούτου), and the ὅπως-clause with the subjunctive gives the content of the request. δρομαῖος is an adjective where English wants an adverb, "at a run".

sentences.t: Ὁ δ’ οὐκ ἄλλως ἔφη τοῦτο ποιήσειν, ἐὰν μὴ τῶν οἰκείων ἐτῶν μέρος αὐτῷ δῷ.
sentences.tr: Ho d’ ouk allōs ephē touto poiēsein, ean mē tōn oikeiōn etōn meros autōi dōi.
sentences.l: But he said that he would not do this otherwise, unless he should give him a part of his own years.
sentences.i: But the man said he would do it on no other terms: the horse must hand over a share of his own years.
sentences.n: ἔφη with the future infinitive ποιήσειν is indirect statement — "said that he would…". ἐὰν μή with the subjunctive δῷ is the ordinary negative condition looking forward, "unless he gives". οἰκεῖος is what belongs to one's own house, and so simply "one's own".

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ἀσμένως παραχωρήσαντος, παρεγένετο μετ’ οὐ πολὺ καὶ βοῦς, οὐδ’ αὐτὸς δυνάμενος ὑπομένειν τὸν χειμῶνα.
sentences.tr: Tou de asmenōs parachōrēsantos, paregeneto met’ ou poly kai bous, oud’ autos dynamenos hypomenein ton cheimōna.
sentences.l: And he having gladly given way, after not long an ox also arrived, he too not being able to endure the winter.
sentences.i: The horse gladly gave way, and not long after an ox arrived as well, no more able than the horse to endure the winter.
sentences.n: μετ’ οὐ πολύ is "after not much", with χρόνον left out as it always is. παραχωρέω is to step aside and let another have the thing — here, the years. οὐδ’ αὐτός, "he too not", carries the negative across from the horse to the ox.

sentences.t: Ὁμοίως δὲ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου μὴ πρότερον ὑποδέξεσθαι φάσκοντος, ἐὰν μὴ τῶν ἰδίων ἐτῶν ἀριθμόν τινα παράσχῃ, καὶ αὐτὸς μέρος δοὺς ὑπεδέχθη.
sentences.tr: Homoiōs de tou anthrōpou mē proteron hypodexesthai phaskontos, ean mē tōn idiōn etōn arithmon tina paraschēi, kai autos meros dous hypedechthē.
sentences.l: And likewise, the man declaring that he would not take him in sooner, unless he should furnish some number of his own years, he too, having given a part, was taken in.
sentences.i: The man likewise declared that he would not take him in until he handed over some number of his own years; and so the ox too gave a share, and was taken in.
sentences.n: μὴ πρότερον … ἐὰν μή works as a pair: "not sooner … unless", which is English "not until". φάσκω, like ἔφη above, takes the future infinitive for indirect statement. ὑποδέξεσθαι and ὑπεδέχθη are the same verb: ὑποδέχομαι is deponent, so the man's refusal carries its future middle and the ox's reception the aorist passive — the bargain closes on the word it opened with.

sentences.t: Τὸ δὲ τελευταῖον κύων ψύχει διαφθειρόμενος ἧκε, καὶ τοῦ ἰδίου χρόνου μέρος ἀπονείμας σκέπης ἔτυχε.
sentences.tr: To de teleutaion kyōn psychei diaphtheiromenos hēke, kai tou idiou chronou meros aponeimas skepēs etyche.
sentences.l: And at the last a dog, being destroyed by cold, came, and, having assigned a part of his own time, obtained shelter.
sentences.i: Last of all came a dog, perishing of the cold; he made over a part of his own time and got his shelter.
sentences.n: τὸ τελευταῖον is an adverbial accusative, "at the last". ψύχει is a dative of cause. τυγχάνω takes the genitive of what one lights upon or obtains (σκέπης). ἀπονέμω is to portion out, the word for dividing an estate — each animal pays in the same coin.

sentences.t: Οὕτω τε συνέβη τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, ὅταν μὲν ἐν τῷ τοῦ Διὸς χρόνῳ γένωνται, ἀκεραίους τε καὶ ἀγαθοὺς εἶναι· ὅταν δὲ εἰς τὰ τοῦ ἵππου ἔτη γένωνται, ἀλάζονάς τε καὶ ὑψαύχενας εἶναι· ἀφικνουμένους δὲ εἰς τὰ τοῦ βοὸς ἔτη, ἀρχικοὺς ὑπάρχειν· τοὺς δὲ τὸν τοῦ κυνὸς χρόνον ἀνύοντας ὀργίλους καὶ ὑλακτικοὺς γίνεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Houtō te synebē tous anthrōpous, hotan men en tōi tou Dios chronōi genōntai, akeraious te kai agathous einai· hotan de eis ta tou hippou etē genōntai, alazonas te kai hypsauchenas einai· aphiknoumenous de eis ta tou boos etē, archikous hyparchein· tous de ton tou kynos chronon anyontas orgilous kai hylaktikous ginesthai.
sentences.l: And so it came about that men, whenever they come to be in the time of Zeus, are unalloyed and good; but whenever they come into the years of the horse, are braggarts and high-necked; and arriving at the years of the ox, are masterful; while those finishing out the time of the dog become quick to anger and given to barking.
sentences.i: And so it fell out that men, whenever they find themselves in Zeus's own time, are unspoilt and good; when they get into the horse's years they are braggarts and carry their heads high; when they reach the ox's years they are masterful; and those working out the dog's time turn irritable and full of barking.
sentences.n: One governing verb, συνέβη, "it came about", holds all four clauses: everything after it is accusative-and-infinitive. ὅταν with the subjunctive states the recurring case, "whenever it happens that…". ἀκέραιος is "unmixed" — a nature with nothing yet stirred into it, which is exactly what the borrowed years will spoil. ὑψαύχην, "high-necked", is said of a horse holding its head up and of a man giving himself airs; the word carries the horse's bearing into the man along with the horse's years. ἀρχικός is "fit to rule", and so of a man given to taking charge.

sentences.t: Τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ χρήσαιτο ἄν τις πρὸς πρεσβύτην θυμώδη καὶ δύστροπον.
sentences.tr: Toutōi tōi logōi chrēsaito an tis pros presbytēn thymōdē kai dystropon.
sentences.l: This story someone might use against an old man who is hot-tempered and hard to get on with.
sentences.n: χρήσαιτο ἄν is a potential optative, the standing form of this closing; χράομαι takes the dative of what is used. πρός with the accusative here is hostile — the story is aimed at such a man, not merely applicable to him. δύστροπος is "of a difficult turn", awkward to deal with — the dog's years, named.
